item.title: Welcome to Draketown....Unincorporated
item.dc:creator: amber
item.content:encoded:
I know most of the nooks and quite a few of the crannies in northwest Georgia, but the one that will always be closest to my heart is Draketown. For many, this small (unincorporated as the signs will remind you) community straddling the Paulding, Haralson and Carroll County lines is just another "blink and you'll miss it" crossroads one might encounter while travelling from Marietta or Dallas to Bremen or Buchanan, or even Alabama if there's a tractor trailer jackknifed on I-20. If you pass through these days you'll find the obligatory Dollar General across a side road from the long abandoned elementary school. There's a gas station, a Baptist church, and several fallen in buildings that locals can point to when explaining that Draketown used to be thriving and bustling enough to support a post office, bank and even a small college.

Long before that though, the land that would become Draketown was home to Native Americans, specifically the Cherokee, Creek and Muscogee. The Cherokee called the area "Long Leaf," likely referencing the longleaf pine trees common in the region. In the 1800s, after the Native Americans were forced to leave Long Leaf, and all of their lands in northwest Georgia, white settlers gradually moved in. Many came from South Carolina and the far reaches of northeast Georgia, recipients of parcels from the lottery system that carved native land up for white farmers. Still others arrived to prospect for copper and gold. It was copper miners from Ducktown, Tennessee who gave Draketown its eventual name, in a nod to their hometown. A drake is another term for a male duck after all.

The population of Draketown grew from about 100 people in 1896, to close to 300 just over 10 years later in 1907. That may not sound like much, but it was a lot of people for what at the time was a distant village deep in the back country of west Georgia. With this increase in population, a need for higher education was seen, and the Draketown Baptist Institute opened. The school was in operation from about 1905 to 1918, first as the Baptist Preparatory College and later known as the Draketown Baptist Institute. Teachers at the school boarded at the Draketown Hotel, which still stands to this day, though long abandoned, and in quite an advanced state of disrepair. After 1918 the institute closed and a community school was opened in its place. A "new" school building was built in 1955, but closed in 1971 with the opening of Haralson County High School. That 1955 building is the old school house that still stands today across from the aforementioned Dollar General, having been used at various times as a flea market, private residence, and planned movie set.

Other local businesses that dotted the Draketown landscape in those days were a cotton gin and gristmill, a blacksmith shop, and multiple dry goods stores. By the time I grew up there in the 1980s, it was hard to imagine any of those businesses, much less a college, ever existing in such a rural location. My cousin grew up in one of the oldest homes in Draketown, a structure once used as a doctor's office and country hospital. It was hard to picture it as such, even though I knew her family stories.

Her house was the setting for some of the greatest tragedies of my childhood. Were they really tragedies? Of course not, but in my memory they feel significantly more serious and painful than they actually were. First, her house is where I learned that an electric fence really is electric, and that if you ride a bike into one, you're gonna find out exactly how electric. 0/10 do not recommend. The other vivid, and terrifying memory I have of her house actually took place deep in the woods behind the main dwelling. She and I, along with another cousin were playing in the woods and we came across "THE HUGE OLD SCARY HAUNTED HOUSE DEEP IN THE WOODS!" Was it actually huge? No, in fact it was probably no more than three or four rooms. Was it all that far back in the woods? I'm actually quite certain it was no more than 50 yards. But there were a lot of trees and I had tiny legs, so it seemed like miles. Now as to whether or not the house was actually haunted -- that all depends on whether or not you believe in such things. But I'm telling you, I've heard enough observations from other people to believe something was up with that house! One thing it definitely, actually, really was, was scary. We were pretty close to the house when my cousin screamed something about seeing a person or a ghost inside, and she and her other cousin took off running back to her house through the woods. Unfortunately a barbed wire fence stood in between the two houses, and when you're RUNNING FOR YOUR LIFE from woodland demon ghosts, and you're approximately 4-5 years old, you don't have the best skills for navigating a barbed wire fence. So when I ducked under, my hair became caught in a barb. And it wouldn't budge. The only thing my cousin knew to do was run back to her house to get scissors. But terror overtook patience and common sense, so instead I nearly scalped myself, ripping free and leaving a good chunk of my hair on the fence behind.

Of course, not all of my early tragedies took place at my cousin's house. I also earned my first off-schedule tetanus shot in Draketown, this time at my grandparents house, playing in the wood pile. I've since learned that most 5 year olds don't have a family wood pile to play in and I think that's both a blessing and a curse. My grandparents had a giant wood burning heater in their living room you see, and my grandfather was always chopping wood for it and had a sizable wood pile by their house. One thing about me that was as true then as it is today.....I'm going to wear flip flops at all the wrong times. So one day I was playing on the wood pile and I stepped down on a piece of junk wood that still had a nail in it, and flip flops are great for a lot of things, but stopping nails is not one of them.

Admittedly, in spite of all these special memories, I didn't always love Draketown and growing up there. It was too far away from......well, everything. Too far from fun activities when I was a young child. Too far for my friends to want to come over once I got to middle and high school and met kids from all of the other far reaches of Paulding County. My road was dirt and my water was from a well. Winter weather could leave us without electricity for days, with limited ways to escape. But now I look back and realize I had acres and acres of woods to explore. I had the majority of my family on both sides living within just a few miles. I had nowhere to ride a bike, but I owned a go kart by age 5. I know that nighttime silence can be quite loud, but it's the prettiest silence you'll ever hear.

One particular aspect of Draketown that has always impressed me is the ability of such a small community to support a sit-down restaurant. Not a gas station fried chicken and breakfast biscuit stand, but a full service, "please wait to be seated," dining room and waitstaff restaurant. When I was a little kid it was called The Hutch House and it was a traditional country cooking establishment. By the time I was a teenager, ownership had changed and it became an Italian/Greek spot. In later years it became a standard American restaurant called Phat Phil's, and in its current iteration, it's known as Draketown Eats. I haven't had a chance to try it yet, but if it's anything like its sister restaurant, Downtown Eats in Dallas, I'm gonna love it. I've driven past a few times and I'm always happy to see the parking lot nearly full at lunch and dinner time.

While it may not have seemed logical for a small community like Draketown to support a full service restaurant during my childhood when it was so sparsely populated, times, they are a'changin'. The growth of new subdivisions, while slower than in other parts of the outer metro Atlanta area, has been increasing during the last 10-15 years. More and more people are drawn to the lower housing prices, less traffic, and scenic backroads that surround Draketown. And many people have found out the secret that as rural as the area seems, you can still be on Interstate 20 in less than 15 minutes most days, and in Atlanta in less than an hour. As the grandchildren and great-grandchildren of earlier settlers begin to sell off family land, developers are turning small tracts into 4-5 new homesites, so buyers can also take advantage of new builds while still avoiding HOAs and crowded neighborhoods if they choose. But the subdivisions are there too, meaning the kids growing up there today have paved roads for their bikes and scooters, and nearby friends so that socialization isn't such an inconvenience when working parents have to drive you to every friends' house.

So, if you find yourself traveling Georgia Highway 120 between Dallas and Buchanan, or Highway 113 between Temple and Rockmart, you'll pass through Draketown. I promise it won't take long if you want to drive around those backroads for a few minutes and see the old homes still standing, many well over 100 years old. Then take a quick drive through some of the new subdivisions being built, with homes that have the same modern features you'd expect closer to Atlanta. And if you're hungry, take a break at Draketown Eats.

item.title: Big Changes to Georgia Property Taxes
item.dc:creator: amber
item.content:encoded:
If you've been frustrated watching your property tax bill creep up year after year, I've got some really good news for you. Georgia recently passed some significant changes to property tax law, and whether you're a longtime homeowner, a first-time buyer, or someone just considering making a move -- this affects you.

A Little Background

As anyone watching their Zestimate knows, over the past few years, home values across Georgia shot up dramatically. That sounds great on paper, like when you get your property value estimate on your monthly mortgage bill, but it came with a painful side effect -- property tax bills went up right along with those values. In some counties, homeowners were seeing their assessments jump by double digits in a single year. For people on fixed incomes or tight budgets, this became a real hardship. Residents all over Georgia began voicing their frustrations to lawmakers, who decided to make some changes during this legislative session to ease that burden.

I'm going to do my best to explain the changes in clear terms, from one neighbor to another!

The Assessment Cap Is Now Airtight

Earlier this month, Georgia Governor Brian Kemp signed a bill into law that prevents local governments and school districts from opting out of the statewide homestead exemption that caps annual increases to taxable property values at the rate of inflation. What does that mean? Well, back in November 2024, Georgia voters approved a statewide homestead tax exemption update. This original version allowed local governments to opt out, meaning they could still increase taxable property values beyond the current rate of inflation. A large number of municipalities did exactly that, including around two thirds of Georgia's school systems, a third of our counties, and a quarter of our cities. So the protection that voters thought they were getting -- many Georgians weren't actually receiving it.

That loophole is now permanently closed. The inflation cap applies everywhere, no exceptions, no opt-outs.

A Creative New Way to Offset Your Tax Bill

Another change to Georgia's property tax laws gives counties and some cities the option to levy a new 1% local sales tax, with the money generated going toward reducing homeowner property tax bills through homestead exemptions, starting January 1, 2028.

Think of it as spreading the load a little more evenly. Instead of property owners carrying the full weight, everyday purchases made in your city or county will offset the property taxes you pay. Of course many of those purchases will be made by local residents, but some will be made by out of county, and even out of state shoppers. This creative tool gives local governments a new way to bring relief to homeowners, sometimes at the expenses of people who don't even live in your municipality.

You'll No Longer Pay for Someone Else's Mistake

This may have been the most frustrating part of Georgia's property tax laws, and one that most needed to be changed.

Imagine your county incorrectly applies a homestead exemption to your account -- through absolutely no fault of your own -- and then years later they come back and hand you a bill for back taxes. It happened to Georgia homeowners more than you'd think.

The new law now bars tax officials from retroactively billing homeowners for additional property taxes when a homestead exemption was applied incorrectly through no fault of the taxpayer. If the county made the error, the county eats the cost. Period. You will no longer be penalized for someone else's mistake.

Your Vote Now Controls Big Tax Increases

This one is about giving power back to the people, and it's long overdue. Beginning in 2027, local governments and school boards that want to adopt budgets projecting property tax revenue increases beyond a threshold tied to the greater of 3% or inflation will need voter approval first. The only exceptions carved out are for economic growth and declared emergencies.

In simpler terms, your local government can't quietly raise your property taxes beyond a certain point without asking you first. They can't pass a budget under the assumption that property tax revenue will increase over a certain amount unless voters approve it.

Direct Relief Is Also on the Way

On top of all the structural changes, there's immediate help coming as well. The Homeowner Tax Relief Grant will save Georgia homeowners a combined $850 million, applied directly to property tax bills by exempting a portion of a home's value from taxation. It shows up right on your bill -- no application required. It is estimated that homeowners will save around $500 off their property tax bill through this relief.

What Do These Changes Mean for the Real Estate Market?

As your local real estate agent, here's my take.

For buyers, this is genuinely encouraging news. One of the biggest unknowns when purchasing a home is what your tax bill will look like five years down the road. This law makes that a lot more predictable, which makes budgeting for home ownership much more manageable.

For sellers, stable and fair property taxes keep buyers confident and the market healthy. A buyer who isn't scared of runaway tax bills is a buyer who's more likely to make a move.

For current homeowners, you've got more protection, more predictability, and more say in what happens going forward.

One Last Thing

And this is very important -- I'm a real estate agent, not a tax attorney or financial advisor! This article is meant to give you a friendly overview of what's changed. For advice specific to your personal situation, please reach out to a tax professional or your county tax commissioner's office.

And if you have any real estate questions at all -- buying, selling, or just curious about the market -- that's exactly what I'm here for. Don't hesitate to reach out!

item.title: Why Real Estate?
item.dc:creator: amber
item.content:encoded:
When you make a major life change, you'll often see your cheerleaders come out. I have a lot of cheerleaders and I am so thankful for all of them. The friends, family, and even mere acquaintances who are truly happy for you. The few people who have known about my new endeavors and have kept me motivated along the way -- I cannot express how much that has propped me up and kept me going. Along with that also comes the people who care about you, who want only what is best for you, but who have genuine concerns about the path you have chosen. It's true -- there are a lot of real estate agents in my area. And a lot of them are really, really good at what they do, with a lot of experience under their belts. But I know there's room for me here too.

I graduated from college in 2000, with degrees in history and anthropology. Look, I was planning to go to law school at the time. In fact, I just took a year off before taking the LSAT.....it's just been a really, really, really long year. I'm obviously a "seasoned professional" at this point, and yet here I am, just now making the move and announcing my new career with Keller Williams. So why real estate? Why now? I have several tongue in cheek responses I've been tossing out at people -- "It combines two things I love, talking to strangers and snooping around people's houses!" or "Well it was this or mortuary school!"

While both of those statements are at least somewhat true, they aren't exactly what brought me here. I've spent the last 25 years playing Corporate America roulette. The first 15 years I worked in criminal and financial background investigations and due diligence. I started as an online researcher, became somewhat of a product owner, then a business analyst and finally a technical writer. I basically wrote the instructions that told robots what to do. When that job moved to India I decided not to go with it. Next I moved onto a role with a Big 4 Accounting Firm, splitting that time between being an anti-money laundering investigator and billing operations specialist. And at no point during those 25 years at either company, could my parents, husband or closest non-work friends tell you what I did for a living. I was everyone's Chandler Bing. A transponster if you will.

My corporate career had its ups and downs, but all along the way I always felt like there was something else. Something bigger. Something more authentically me. As 2025 began barrelling to its end, I started feeling more and more like I was just treading water at my job. And yet, as God sent me sign after sign that it might be time to jump ship, I dug my heels in and ignored the signs, determined to tread that water even harder! So God got my attention.....by giving me a swift kick out of my comfort zone, in the form of a large-scale corporate layoff. I went through every stage of job grief -- anger, regret, depression, terror, acceptance, motivation. I updated my Linked In and polished up my resume. And then I froze. I found hundreds of jobs in my field just waiting for me to apply. But in my gut, in the pit of my stomach, I knew that wasn't the path I was supposed to take. I believe that it's human nature to remain where you are comfortable. My schedule was flexible, the money was decent and the stress was manageable. That's about as comfortable as a person can be in that industry.

Meanwhile, my husband has spent the better part of the last 20 years telling me I need to be a real estate agent. I always chuckled at it as a compliment, but largely ignored him, even though he knows a thing or two about the industry, having worked adjacent to the real estate business for most of those 20 years. He has told me repeatedly that my extroverted personality, my ability to talk to anyone and everyone, mixed with my research skills and the strange combination of experience I've gotten over the years that blends finance with contracts with law with property records.....all of those things make this the exactly right industry for me he would say.

"BUT I DONT DO SALES!!"

I protested for years, believing that while everything he said sounded right, he was forgetting the one very important aspect of my personality. I don't do sales. He calmly pointed out that selling MYSELF is literally what I do whenever I walk into a room full of strangers, though I tend to call them "potential new best friends." And what he referred to as "selling myself" is to me just "welcoming everyone to the Amber Show." Asking them to grab a seat and get ready to be entertained. Offering nonrefundable subscriptions even. In spite of all of his valid points, he was easy to ignore when my steady corporate paycheck was whispering in my other ear. When I was comfortable.

So now, I've finally stopped ignoring him. About this anyway. I decided instead to jump headfirst into a completely new world. I've worked hard for 25 years. (Really, it's more like 31 years, because by golly, I gave it my all....well OK, I gave it my some....at Winn Dixie and Johnny's BBQ and Walmart in high school.) Alas, those locales will be the backdrops of future posts I'm sure. But I've decided that if I'm going to continue to work that hard, I'm going to be doing that work for myself. For someone who won't lay me off on a corporate whim. Is it scary? Of course. I'm terrified. But I'm also very, very excited for this new chapter. So to those who have expressed concern....yes, I do know that the real estate agent market is both saturated and competitive. I know that for some potential clients, experience will matter more than my intoxicating personality and tenacious dedication to securing the best deal possible. And that's OK. Because there's still room for me here. Get in where you fit in after all!
